samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On September 18, 2023, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) released its “Pathways to Commercial Liftoff: Industrial Decarbonization” report. [1] The report warns that the nation's heavy industries are at risk of failing to meet the Biden administration's climate goals and lagging behind international progress. [1] It highlights that achieving a net-zero economy by 2050 will necessitate between $700 billion and $1 trillion in public and private investment for industrial decarbonization. The document outlines that deployable and demonstration-ready technologies could abate 25-40% of emissions by 2030, but require cost reductions to be economically viable. [5] Another 25% of abatement could come from technologies with positive economics, while factors like grid decarbonization could contribute about 140 million metric tons of CO2 reduction. [5] The report is part of a series intended to create a dialogue between the public and private sectors to speed up the deployment of clean energy technologies in key industries like steel, cement, and aluminum. [1, 8] <2> On July 20, 2023, the Colorado Air Quality Control Commission (AQCC) unanimously approved a new, first-of-its-kind rule requiring the direct measurement and verification of methane emissions from oil and gas production facilities. This regulation mandates that operators calculate their greenhouse gas intensity—the ratio of emissions to the amount of oil and gas produced—and use direct measurements to inform their emissions inventory. The rule is part of a broader effort to ensure compliance with Colorado's 2021 greenhouse gas intensity standards and to meet state-mandated emission reduction targets for 2025 and 2030. While it received broad consensus support from environmental groups, local governments, and industry stakeholders, some environmental advocates expressed concern that the timelines for reporting and oversight might be too slow to verify pollution levels before 2027. The regulation requires certain operators to have their emissions data reviewed by an independent, third-party auditor certified by the state's Air Pollution Control Division. <3> A report from the Net Zero Tracker initiative, published in June 2023, revealed that a significant number of large corporations are failing to meet the basic integrity requirements of their own 2050 net-zero emissions pledges. The analysis, titled "Net Zero Stocktake 2023", examined over 1,000 companies with net-zero targets from the world's 2,000 largest publicly-listed firms and found that only 4% have commitments that meet the UN's 'Starting Line criteria'. These criteria are designed to ensure pledges are credible and aligned with the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. While the number of companies setting net-zero targets has more than doubled in just over two years, the report highlights a major gap in the quality and credibility of these commitments, with only 37% of corporate targets fully covering Scope 3 emissions. <4> In the first quarter of 2023, venture capital investment in carbon and emissions technology companies demonstrated resilience, reaching $3.6 billion across 212 deals. According to a report from PitchBook, this represented a 35% increase in investment value year-over-year, although it was a 13% decline from the fourth quarter of 2022. A notable highlight within the sector was building energy efficiency, which saw its highest-ever quarterly VC investment value in Q1 2023. <5> On May 10, 2023, Rhode Island's Governor Dan McKee announced that the Department of Environmental Management (DEM) filed regulations to adopt California's Advanced Clean Cars II (ACCII) and Advanced Clean Trucks (ACT) standards. This initiative mandates that by 2035, all new passenger cars and light-duty trucks sold in Rhode Island must be zero-emission vehicles. The regulations, which also apply to manufacturers and not directly to consumers or dealers, will phase in, requiring an increasing percentage of zero-emission vehicle sales starting in model year 2027. This action aligns Rhode Island with other states, including Massachusetts, New York, Vermont, Washington, Virginia, and Oregon, which have also adopted California's more stringent emissions standards under the provisions of the federal Clean Air Act. The move is a key component of Rhode Island's strategy to meet the mandates of its Act on Climate, which targets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, as the transportation sector accounts for approximately 40% of the state's emissions. <6> A report from the National Caucus of Environmental Legislators (NCEL), not the National Center for Environmental Information as originally claimed, highlighted significant state-level legislative efforts to decarbonize buildings in 2023. As of May 3, 2023, at least 147 bills had been introduced across 24 states aiming to lower emissions and enhance energy efficiency in residential and commercial buildings. The report confirmed that among these states, Colorado and Utah had already enacted new laws. Colorado's H.B.1134 requires home warranty companies to offer electric appliance replacements for gas-powered ones, while Utah's H.B.217 authorized grants for schools to reduce energy and water consumption.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On March 12, 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced its plan to propose a new rule in the spring of 2025 aimed at reconsidering the 'Clean Power Plan 2.0'. The regulation, which the EPA's announcement refers to as the 'Biden-Harris Rule', focuses on establishing standards and guidelines for greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants. <2> As part of its 'Transition 2025' series, the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) held a panel discussion on March 5, 2025, titled 'The Future of U.S. Climate and Energy Policy'. The discussion centered on potential policy changes under a new Trump administration, drawing lessons from his first term and examining likely shifts from the Biden administration's policies. Panelists, including Alice Hill of the CFR and Michael Catanzaro of the CGCN Group, explored the future trajectories of U.S. energy sectors like oil, solar, wind, and natural gas. The event was moderated by Justin Worland, a senior correspondent for TIME. This event is distinct from the Heritage Foundation's 'Project 2025' initiative. <3> On February 28, 2025, the Carbon Capture Coalition, a nonpartisan group of over 100 organizations, released its 2025 Federal Policy Blueprint. [1, 6] The document presents a consensus-based roadmap of policy recommendations for the 119th Congress and the administration to support the commercial-scale deployment of carbon management technologies nationwide. [1] The blueprint addresses the full suite of technologies, including carbon capture from industrial facilities and power plants, direct air capture, and the transport, utilization, and storage of CO2. [3, 5] While supportive policies like the 45Q tax credit have spurred the announcement of over 270 projects, the Coalition notes that inflationary pressures and other economic factors create headwinds. [1, 6] The blueprint's recommendations aim to ensure these announced projects are realized and help the nation meet its deployment goals, which require a significant scaling of carbon capture capacity by 2030. [4, 6] Key policy areas include enhancing the 45Q tax credit, improving permitting systems, expanding carbon markets, and investing in next-generation technologies. [2, 5] <4> In early 2025, legislators in New York and Colorado introduced bills to mandate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions disclosures for large corporations. On January 27, 2025, New York introduced Senate Bill S3456, the 'climate corporate data accountability act.' This legislation targets companies with annual revenues exceeding $1 billion, requiring them to begin reporting Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions in 2027 and Scope 3 emissions in 2028. Similarly, Colorado's House Bill 25-1119 was introduced in January 2025 with a comparable $1 billion revenue threshold, proposing disclosure of Scope 1 and 2 emissions, with Scope 3 reporting to be phased in starting in 2029. However, the Colorado bill was indefinitely postponed by the House Energy & Environment Committee on February 27, 2025. <5> In a December 2024 interagency report submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the U.S. government provided its latest official projections for national greenhouse gas emissions. The document, titled the 'First Biennial Transparency Report', forecasts a net decline in U.S. greenhouse gas emissions of 36-57% by 2035, compared to 2005 levels. These projections, compiled by the Environmental Protection Agency, Department of Energy, and Department of Agriculture, incorporate the effects of federal policies enacted through May 2024, including the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL), and recently finalized standards for vehicles, power plants, oil and gas production, and appliances. <6> The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has issued a final action that denies or partially denies two petitions for reconsideration concerning the greenhouse gas standards for new, modified, and reconstructed fossil fuel-fired power plants. The notice, published in the Federal Register, responds to petitions submitted by Mountain State Energy Holdings and the Edison Electric Institute regarding the "New Source Performance Standards for Greenhouse Gas Emissions From New, Modified, and Reconstructed Fossil Fuel-Fired Electric Generating Units; Emission Guidelines for Greenhouse Gas Emissions From Existing Fossil Fuel-Fired Electric Generating Units; and Repeal of the Affordable Clean Energy Rule" which was originally published on May 9, 2024. The EPA's decision, effective January 15, 2025, denies reconsideration on several grounds raised by the petitioners, including issues related to grid reliability, financial assertions about new baseload gas plants, and the enforceable backstop emissions rate for coal-fired plants. The basis for the denial is detailed in a separate document available in the rulemaking docket. This action is considered nationally applicable, and any petitions for review must be filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit by March 17, 2025. <7> On December 20, 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) jointly announced that 43 projects were selected for negotiation to receive approximately $850 million in funding. This initiative is a key part of the broader Methane Emissions Reduction Program, funded by the Inflation Reduction Act, which will provide up to $1.36 billion in total financial and technical assistance. The funding aims to reduce methane pollution from the oil and gas sector by improving the monitoring, measurement, and quantification of emissions. The program specifically targets providing assistance to small oil and gas operators and Tribes, helping them to deploy commercially available and innovative technologies to mitigate methane releases. The National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL) of the DOE will manage the selected projects. <8> On December 20, 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) announced a $51.7 million investment for 19 projects aimed at advancing innovative transportation technologies to expand affordable and reliable mobility options. The initiative, part of the Fiscal Year 2024 Vehicle Technologies Office Research & Development funding program, will focus on a wide range of next-generation technologies. Key areas of research include developing electric vehicle (EV) battery technologies with domestic, low-cost materials like phosphate-based cathodes and sodium-ion batteries, improving off-road vehicle technology, advancing vehicle-to-everything (V2X) connectivity, creating domestically produced electrical steels for powertrains, and strengthening cybersecurity for EV charging infrastructure. <9> On December 19, 2024, the Biden administration announced a new Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) for the United States, submitting it to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). [1, 5, 7, 10] The updated target commits to an economy-wide reduction of net greenhouse gas emissions by 61-66% below 2005 levels by the year 2035. [1, 6] This plan also specifically anticipates a methane reduction of at least 35% from 2005 levels by 2035. [6, 8] The announcement and submission were made just a month before the end of the administration, with the goal of keeping the U.S. on a path to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 and maintaining the global goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. [4, 10] The submission was one of a handful made before a largely symbolic UN deadline of February 10, 2025, for new 2035 climate plans. [9, 11, 12] <10> A Pew Research Center survey of 9,593 U.S. adults, conducted from October 21-27, 2024, revealed broad American support for policies aimed at addressing climate change. The findings, published on December 9, 2024, show that 83% of Americans favor tax credits for individuals who improve their home's energy efficiency, and 79% support tax credits for businesses developing carbon capture technologies. Additionally, the survey highlighted widespread political frustration, with 80% of Americans reporting they feel frustrated about the level of political disagreement on the issue of climate change.

Residential sector emissions fell by 3% (10 MMmt), largely due to decreased demand for heating fuels during a relatively warm late-winter and early-spring. Industrial sector CO2 emissions decreased by 1% (14 MMmt), a change associated with a slowdown in industrial production and manufacturing growth. In contrast, emissions from the transportation and electric power sectors remained relatively unchanged. This downturn directly followed the expiration of federal EV tax credits, worth up to $7,500 for new vehicles, on September 30, 2025. The impending deadline had created a surge in sales in the preceding months as automakers held campaigns to clear inventory and consumers rushed to take advantage of the savings, effectively pulling future sales into the second and third quarters. Other analysts, including J.D. Power and S&P Global Mobility, also reported a similar collapse in EV market share for October, with estimates around 5-5.2%. <3> A U.S. federal government shutdown began at midnight on October 1, 2025, after Congress failed to pass the necessary appropriations legislation for the 2026 fiscal year. This resulted in the furlough of approximately 900,000 federal employees and left many others working without pay. The shutdown, which became the longest in U.S. history, had widespread implications. Impacts included the closure of national parks, capital museums, and other public institutions, potential disruptions to food assistance programs like SNAP, and significant travel delays as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) reduced flights due to air traffic controller staffing shortages. The GHGRP, established in 2009, requires over 8,000 facilities to report their annual greenhouse gas emissions. The EPA stated that the program is burdensome, costly, and not essential for fulfilling its statutory obligations under the Clean Air Act. The agency estimated that rescinding the program would save regulated entities up to $2.4 billion over ten years. The proposal would leave reporting requirements only for natural gas systems covered by the Waste Emissions Charge (WEC), with these requirements delayed until 2034. This action is part of a broader environmental deregulation initiative. The announcement was met with criticism from some members of Congress, who argued that the EPA is violating congressional directives and undermining transparency and data-driven climate policy. <5> Two separate announcements from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) occurred on different dates. On October 29, 2025, the DOE announced a Notice of Funding Opportunity for up to $100 million to refurbish and modernize the nation's existing coal power plants.
